title: Mark 7:31–37
context: After traveling through the Decapolis region, Jesus personally restores a man’s hearing and speech. Both traditions recognize his compassionate authority, while Mark’s account distinguishes the crowd’s amazement from obedience to Jesus’ command.

verses.text: Again he departed from the borders of Tyre and Sidon, and came to the sea of Galilee through the middle of the region of Decapolis.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus returns toward the sea of Galilee through the Decapolis region. Arminian readers see the continuing movement beyond the setting of the earlier purity dispute, with another act of restoration soon to follow.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise attend to Mark’s geographical transition without inferring the identity of every person present. The narrative prepares another display of Jesus’ compassionate authority.

verses.text: They brought to him one who was deaf and had an impediment in his speech. They begged him to lay his hand on him.
verses.arminianNotes: Others bring a man who cannot hear and has difficulty speaking, asking Jesus to touch him. Arminian readers see the practical love of those who help a vulnerable neighbor approach Christ.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise recognize intercession and human care as part of the encounter. The request looks to Jesus’ power rather than to the man’s ability to explain his own need.

verses.text: He took him aside from the multitude privately and put his fingers into his ears; and he spat and touched his tongue.
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus takes the man aside and uses bodily gestures directed to his ears and tongue. Arminian readers see personal, concrete care rather than treatment of the man as a public spectacle.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers also emphasize Christ’s attentive condescension to bodily need. These particular actions describe his freedom to heal; they do not establish a technique that others can control or reproduce at will.

verses.text: Looking up to heaven, he sighed, and said to him, “Ephphatha!” that is, “Be opened!”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus looks toward heaven, sighs, and commands the man to be opened. Arminian readers see compassion joined to dependence on the Father; Mark supplies the meaning of Ephphatha within the verse.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers stress the authority of Jesus’ command while sharing the emphasis on his compassionate sigh. The healing is personal and purposeful, not a detached exhibition of power.

verses.text: Immediately his ears were opened, and the impediment of his tongue was released, and he spoke clearly.
verses.arminianNotes: The man immediately hears and speaks clearly. Arminian readers see a gracious restoration of communication and participation in ordinary life, not a reward for a specified achievement.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise emphasize that Christ’s word effectively accomplishes the bodily healing. The event displays his authority without requiring every detail to become an allegory of conversion.

verses.text: He commanded them that they should tell no one, but the more he commanded them, so much the more widely they proclaimed it.
verses.arminianNotes: The spreading report directly conflicts with Jesus’ command to remain silent. Arminian readers note that enthusiasm is not the same as obedience, even when the news being shared is true.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise distinguish amazement from submission to Christ’s direction. Mark records the widening fame without presenting disobedience as a model for faithful witness.

verses.text: They were astonished beyond measure, saying, “He has done all things well. He makes even the deaf hear and the mute speak!”
verses.arminianNotes: The crowd marvels at Jesus’ restoration of hearing and speech. Arminian readers see praise arising from tangible mercy, while the wider story will show that amazement alone does not equal mature faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers share the joy in Christ’s good work and the caution about confusing wonder with understanding. The opened ears also sharpen the coming question of whether the disciples themselves truly hear.
